react.name: React
react.tagline: Describe the screen as functions of state, and let React work out the changes.
react.rendering: client, or server with a framework
pipeline: Write components in JSX
A build step turns JSX into function calls
react and react-dom ship to the browser
State changes re-run components; React diffs and patches the DOM
what: React describes a screen as a tree of components. A component is a function that takes props and returns what that part of the screen should look like, written in JSX, which looks like HTML inside JavaScript. State lives in hooks such as useState.
React is a library, not a full framework: it draws the UI and leaves routing, data loading and the build to you or to a framework built on it, of which Next.js is the biggest.
how: When state changes, React calls the component again and gets a new description of the UI. It compares that tree with the previous one (the virtual DOM, reconciled by an algorithm called Fiber) and changes only the real DOM nodes that differ.
Rendering can be paused, resumed and prioritised, which is what concurrent rendering means. Hooks keep state per component instance, so the order of hook calls must not change between renders.
Server Components are components that run only on the server and send their output to the client, so their code never ships to the browser. They need a framework or bundler that supports them.
good: The largest ecosystem and hiring pool of the frameworks here
One model for the web and, with React Native, for mobile
Very flexible: you pick the router, data layer and build
costs: The runtime ships to every visitor (see the measured figure)
You assemble the rest of the stack yourself, or adopt a framework that has
Re-running components on every change means unnecessary re-renders are the developer’s to find and prevent
overlap: Preact implements the same API in a much smaller package, and preact/compat lets many React libraries run on it.
Next.js is a framework built on React, and supplies the routing, server rendering and bundling React leaves out.
Solid uses JSX too, so code looks alike, but it does not re-run components.
differs: Svelte moves the work to build time: a compiler writes the DOM updates, with no diffing at run time.
Vue tracks which state each component reads and re-renders only that component, so developers rarely write memoization by hand.
react.pros: Large community, reusable components, robust ecosystem.
react.cons: Requires JSX and build tooling, steeper learning curve.

preact.name: Preact
preact.tagline: React’s API in a small package.
pipeline: Write components in JSX
A build step turns JSX into function calls
preact ships to the browser
State changes re-run components; Preact diffs and patches the DOM
what: Preact is a lightweight alternative to React that keeps the same component and hooks API. It is made to be small, and its compatibility layer, preact/compat, lets many React libraries run on it.
It also offers signals in a separate package, which are reactive values that update the parts of the UI that read them without re-running whole components.
how: Preact’s diffing works on the same idea as React’s virtual DOM. It leaves out features such as React’s concurrent scheduling and synthetic event system, which is where the saving in size comes from.
Many tools, Astro among them, accept Preact as a drop-in for React in places where the bundle size matters.
good: React’s model at a fraction of the download (see the measured figure)
Most React libraries work through the compatibility layer
Fast to start
costs: Not every React feature or library behaves identically
Smaller team and ecosystem than React
Newest React features reach it later, or not at all
overlap: Same API, same JSX, same hooks.
A common choice for Astro islands.
differs: Preact still re-runs components and diffs; Solid does not.
preact.pros: React’s model at a fraction of the download (see the measured figure). Most React libraries work through the compatibility layer.
preact.cons: Not every React feature or library behaves identically. Smaller team and ecosystem than React.

solid.name: Solid
solid.tagline: React’s look with no re-rendering: signals update only what read them.
pipeline: Write components in JSX
The compiler turns JSX into direct DOM creation and signal subscriptions
A small reactive runtime ships
A signal change updates the exact DOM node that read it
what: Solid looks like React: components are functions and the markup is JSX. The difference is that a component function runs once. The state it creates, with createSignal, is a reactive value, and the places in the JSX that read it become subscriptions.
SolidStart is the application framework for routing and server rendering.
how: The JSX compiler turns each expression in the markup into an effect that reads signals. When a signal changes, only those effects run and the matching DOM nodes are updated; no component function is called again and no tree is compared.
This is why reading a signal in Solid means calling it, count(), and why destructuring props can lose reactivity.
good: Updates are targeted by construction
React-like syntax eases the move for React developers
Small runtime
costs: A far smaller ecosystem than React’s
Habits from React (destructuring props, conditionals in JSX) can silently break reactivity
A younger framework ecosystem and tooling
overlap: Both update the DOM without a virtual DOM.
differs: In React the component function re-runs on change; in Solid it runs once.
Vue tracks reads per component render; Solid tracks per expression.
solid.pros: Updates are targeted by construction. React-like syntax eases the move for React developers.
solid.cons: A far smaller ecosystem than React’s. Habits from React (destructuring props, conditionals in JSX) can silently break reactivity.

lit.name: Lit
lit.tagline: A small layer over the browser’s own component standard.
pipeline: Write a class that extends LitElement
Register it as a custom element
A small library ships
A property change re-evaluates the template and updates only the changed parts
what: Lit builds components out of the browser’s own Web Components standards: custom elements, shadow DOM and templates. A Lit component is a class registered as an HTML tag, so it works in any page and inside any other framework.
It is the successor to the Polymer project at Google.
how: The template is a JavaScript tagged template literal, html`...`. The first render creates the DOM; after that, when a reactive property changes, Lit re-evaluates the template and updates only the parts of the DOM that hold changed values, with no virtual DOM tree.
Because the result is a real custom element, there is no framework boundary to cross: a Lit element can be used from React, Vue, Angular or plain HTML.
good: Components that work everywhere
Very small library on top of platform features
Styles are scoped by the browser, with shadow DOM
costs: No router, store or full-stack story of its own
Shadow DOM makes global styling and some form handling harder
Server rendering is less mature than the meta-frameworks’
overlap: Astro can host Lit components as islands.
A Lit element can be used inside React.
differs: Lit components are browser elements, React components are not.
Svelte compiles components away; Lit keeps a small runtime and uses the platform.
lit.pros: Components that work everywhere. Very small library on top of platform features.
lit.cons: No router, store or full-stack story of its own. Shadow DOM makes global styling and some form handling harder.

vue.name: Vue
vue.lang: JavaScript or TypeScript, with single-file components
vue.tagline: Templates and reactive state that you can adopt a piece at a time.
pipeline: Write a .vue file: template, script and style together
The compiler turns the template into optimised render functions
vue ships to the browser
A change to reactive state re-renders only the components that read it
what: Vue is a framework for building interfaces from components. Each component is usually one .vue file with a <template> written in HTML-like syntax, a <script> and optionally a <style>. It is described as progressive: it can be added to one page with a script tag, or used as a full build-tooled app.
The official router (Vue Router) and state store (Pinia) are separate packages that the project maintains alongside the core.
how: Vue 3 wraps state in reactive proxies. While a component renders, Vue records which reactive values it reads; when one of those changes, only the components that read it are scheduled to render again. The developer rarely writes memoization.

Templates are compiled ahead of time. The compiler marks which parts of a template are static and which can change, so the update step skips the static parts. Under the hood there is still a virtual DOM; Vapor Mode is an in-development compile mode that drops it.
good: Gentle to adopt: HTML-like templates, one file per component
Fine-grained updates without hand-written optimisation
Official router, store and build tool (Vite, also made by Evan You) that fit together
costs: Two ways to write components (Options API and Composition API) coexist
A smaller job market and library catalogue than React
Templates are a separate language from JavaScript, which is a gain for some teams and a loss for others
overlap: Both use single-file components with an HTML-like template, compiled ahead of time.
Nuxt is the full-stack framework on top of Vue.
Both use HTML templates with directives for loops and conditions.
differs: React’s model is re-run the function and diff; Vue’s is track what was read and update just that.
Solid tracks reads too, but at the level of single expressions, with no component re-render and no virtual DOM.
vue.pros: Easy to learn, flexible, and highly approachable.
vue.cons: Smaller ecosystem compared to React, less corporate backing.

angular.name: Angular
angular.tagline: A complete, opinionated platform: components, router, forms, HTTP and dependency injection.
angular.claim: The whole platform in one box
angular.rendering: client, or server with built-in SSR
pipeline: Write components as TypeScript classes with templates
The Angular compiler turns templates into code ahead of time
A bundle with the runtime ships to the browser
Signals and change detection update the DOM
what: Angular is a framework that comes with almost everything an application needs: a component model, a router, form handling, an HTTP client, testing tools and a command-line tool. It is written in TypeScript and requires it.
Angular 2 (2016) was a rewrite of AngularJS, the earlier framework from 2010 which shares its name and is a different thing. Its creators include Miško Hevery, who later made Qwik.
how: Components are classes with a decorator that names an HTML template. Services are classes provided through dependency injection: a component asks for what it needs and the framework supplies it.

Angular compiles templates ahead of time. Updating the screen has historically relied on zone.js, which notices asynchronous events and triggers change detection over the component tree. Signals are a newer reactive primitive that tell Angular exactly which bindings changed, and the framework is moving toward updates driven by signals instead of zones.
good: Everything is included and designed to fit together
Strong conventions help large teams keep code alike
Typed from templates to services
costs: The most concepts to learn first: modules or standalone components, injection, decorators, RxJS
Starts larger than the small libraries, because the platform comes with it (see the measured figure)
Opinionated: leaving its conventions is harder than in a library
overlap: HTML templates with directives for conditions and loops.
Created by the same person (Miško Hevery), with the opposite answer on how much work to do at start-up.
differs: React is one library of UI parts; Angular is a platform that decides the router, forms and HTTP client for you.
Svelte ships little runtime; Angular ships a framework.
angular.pros: Comprehensive framework, built-in TypeScript support, two-way data binding.
angular.cons: Verbose syntax, steep learning curve, heavy structure.

svelte.name: Svelte
svelte.tagline: A compiler that turns components into direct DOM updates.
svelte.claim: Does its work at build time
pipeline: Write a .svelte file
The compiler turns it into JavaScript that updates the DOM directly
Only that output and a small runtime ship
A change runs just the code for what depended on it
what: Svelte is a compiler. A .svelte file holds markup, script and style, and the build turns it into plain JavaScript that creates and updates the DOM, so less of a framework has to be sent to the browser.
SvelteKit is the application framework around it: file-based routes, server rendering, form handling and adapters for deploying to different hosts.
how: Svelte 5 introduced runes, such as $state and $derived, to mark reactive values. The compiler sees where each is used and writes code that updates only those places when they change; there is no virtual DOM to diff.

Because the work is decided at build time, a small component can compile to very little code. The cost is that the compiler is part of the toolchain, and a component’s reactivity is understood by reading the compiler’s rules.
good: Small output for small apps (see the measured figure)
Little boilerplate: state is a variable
SvelteKit supplies routing and rendering modes
costs: A smaller ecosystem and fewer jobs than React or Angular
A compiler step and its own syntax, which tools must support
The runes model replaced the earlier reactive syntax, so older tutorials differ
overlap: Both do fine-grained updates with no virtual DOM, Solid at run time through signals and Svelte mostly at compile time.
differs: React sends a runtime that diffs; Svelte sends compiled updates.
Angular ships the platform; Svelte ships the component.
svelte.pros: Compiles to efficient vanilla JavaScript, minimal runtime overhead, simple syntax.
svelte.cons: Smaller community, less mature tooling and ecosystem.

qwik.name: Qwik
qwik.tagline: Do not run the app again in the browser: resume where the server stopped.
qwik.claim: Picks up where the server stopped
pipeline: Write components in JSX with $ boundaries
The optimizer splits code at each $ into lazy chunks
The server sends HTML with state and listeners serialised into it
A tiny loader fetches only the code an interaction needs
what: Qwik is built around resumability. Other server-rendering frameworks send HTML and then re-run the application in the browser to attach listeners and rebuild state. Qwik serialises that information into the HTML on the server, so the browser can continue from there without re-running anything.
Qwik City is its application framework, with file-based routing and server data loaders.
how: Any function the author marks with a $ suffix, such as onClick$, becomes a boundary that the build can move into its own file. The page loads a very small script, the Qwikloader, which listens for events; when one fires it downloads just the code for that handler.

So the JavaScript that loads with the page is nearly constant however large the app is, and the JavaScript for a feature arrives when the user reaches for it. The cost shows after the first click, which is why this site measures both.
good: Built so that start-up cost need not grow with the app (not shown by a counter, which is too small)
Code for a feature loads when used
Familiar JSX and signals
costs: Developers must learn the $ rules about what can be serialised
A small ecosystem and few libraries built for it
First interactions can wait on a network request for their code
overlap: Both render on the server and send HTML first.
differs: Next.js hydrates, re-running client components in the browser; Qwik resumes without that step.
Its author’s earlier project: Angular ships a framework up front, Qwik delays everything it can.
qwik.pros: Built so that start-up cost need not grow with the app (not shown by a counter, which is too small). Code for a feature loads when used.
qwik.cons: Developers must learn the $ rules about what can be serialised. A small ecosystem and few libraries built for it.

nextjs.name: Next.js
nextjs.tagline: React plus the parts React leaves out: routes, servers, bundling and data.
pipeline: Folders under app/ become routes
Each route is rendered on the server or at build time
HTML, then the React client code, reach the browser
React hydrates the page and takes over interaction
what: Next.js is a framework built on React. Its router is the file system: a folder becomes a URL, and special files in it (page, layout) say what to draw. It adds server rendering, static generation, API endpoints, image and font handling, and its own bundler.
In the App Router, components are Server Components by default. A file marked 'use client' becomes a Client Component, which is the kind used for state and interaction.
how: For each route Next.js decides when its HTML is made: at build time (static), on each request (dynamic), or a mixture with cached results that are refreshed. The server sends HTML first, so the page shows before any JavaScript runs.

The browser then downloads the React runtime and the Client Components on the page, and React hydrates the HTML: it attaches event handlers to the markup already there instead of drawing it again. Layouts stay mounted while the user moves between routes, and Server Actions let a form call a server function directly.
good: One tool for pages, routes, rendering modes and deployment
Search-friendly HTML from the first response
Big ecosystem, because React’s is its own
costs: It inherits React’s runtime and adds its own (see the measured figure)
Several rendering modes and caching layers must be understood to predict behaviour
Built around React and, in practice, around one hosting company’s platform
overlap: Every Next.js component is a React component, and React libraries work in it.
Nuxt does for Vue what Next.js does for React: file routing, server rendering, hybrid rendering per route.
Both can produce static HTML for content pages.
differs: Astro ships no JavaScript by default and hydrates only chosen islands, where Next.js hydrates the Client Components on a page.
Qwik resumes where the server stopped instead of hydrating, so it needs no start-up re-run.
nextjs.pros: One tool for pages, routes, rendering modes and deployment. Search-friendly HTML from the first response.
nextjs.cons: It inherits React’s runtime and adds its own (see the measured figure). Several rendering modes and caching layers must be understood to predict behaviour.

nuxt.name: Nuxt
nuxt.tagline: Vue with routing, server rendering and a server built in.
nuxt.claim: Vue, built for the full stack
pipeline: Files under pages/ become routes
The Nitro server renders HTML for each route
HTML and the Vue client code reach the browser
Vue hydrates and takes over
what: Nuxt is the framework for building complete applications with Vue. It gives file-based routing, layouts, data-fetching helpers, automatic imports of components and composables, and a server layer.
Its server engine is Nitro, which can output a Node server, static files or functions for many hosting platforms from the same code.
how: Each route can be rendered on the server per request, at build time, or on the client only, set per route with route rules. The server sends HTML, and Vue then hydrates it in the browser.
Because routes and components are found by convention, most of the wiring a Vue app would need (router setup, imports) is generated for you.
good: A full-stack Vue app with little configuration
Rendering mode chosen per route
Deploys to many hosts from one code base
costs: Convention and auto-imports hide code paths that a plain Vue app shows
Adds a server runtime and build step to Vue’s own
Smaller than Next.js in community and hosting integrations
overlap: The same job for a different view library: routing, rendering modes, server code.
differs: Nuxt’s Vue reactivity rarely needs hand-written memoization, and its auto-imports remove import lines that Next.js code spells out.
Astro sends no framework runtime unless a page asks for an island.
nuxt.pros: A full-stack Vue app with little configuration. Rendering mode chosen per route.
nuxt.cons: Convention and auto-imports hide code paths that a plain Vue app shows. Adds a server runtime and build step to Vue’s own.

astro.name: Astro
astro.by: Fred K. Schott and the Astro team
astro.lang: Astro components, with JavaScript or TypeScript
astro.tagline: Static HTML by default, with islands of interactivity where you ask for them.
astro.claim: No JS until a part needs it
astro.updates: none on the page; islands use their own framework
pipeline: Pages are .astro files that render to HTML at build time
A UI component marked client:* becomes an island
HTML ships; only the islands’ JavaScript ships
Each island hydrates on load, when visible or when idle
what: Astro is a framework for sites that are mostly content: blogs, docs, marketing and shops. A page is rendered to plain HTML at build time and no JavaScript is sent unless a component needs it.
It does not have its own component model for interactivity. An interactive piece, called an island, is written in React, Preact, Vue, Svelte, Solid or Lit, and may be mixed on the same page.
how: A directive such as client:load or client:visible tells Astro when to hydrate an island. The rest of the page stays inert HTML.
Content collections give Markdown and data files a typed schema, and adapters allow server rendering when a page needs it.
good: Content pages with no JavaScript cost
Use the UI library you already know, or several
Fast static output
costs: Not made for highly interactive, app-like pages
State shared between islands needs extra care
Mixing libraries means shipping each one’s runtime
overlap: A common choice for the interactive islands.
Both can emit static HTML for content pages.
differs: Next.js hydrates its whole React tree for a page; Astro hydrates only the islands.
Both avoid shipping everything up front, by opposite means: Astro by not sending, Qwik by deferring.
astro.pros: Content pages with no JavaScript cost. Use the UI library you already know, or several.
astro.cons: Not made for highly interactive, app-like pages. State shared between islands needs extra care.

htmx.name: htmx
htmx.tagline: Ask the server for HTML and put it where you say, with attributes.
htmx.updates: swap HTML fragments from the server
pipeline: Add hx-* attributes to HTML
One small script ships
An event sends a request to the server
The server answers with an HTML fragment, which htmx swaps into the page
what: htmx extends HTML so that any element can make a request and any response can replace part of the page. hx-post says which request to make, and hx-target and hx-swap say where the answer goes.
It succeeds intercooler.js, by the same author, and is built on the idea of hypermedia: the server returns HTML, not JSON, and the page changes by exchanging HTML.
how: The server holds the state and does the rendering, in whatever language it already uses. The browser holds the script and the markup. A click sends a request, the server replies with a fragment of HTML, and htmx swaps it in.
It needs no build step and no client-side component model, which is also what it gives up: the page cannot respond to a click without a round trip, unless other script is written.
good: No build, no client state to keep in sync
Works with any backend language
Small single script
costs: Every interaction that changes state needs a server round trip
Rich client-only interactions (drag, offline, optimistic UI) need other tools
State and logic live on the server, so the server must be there
overlap: Both favour mostly-HTML pages with a little interactivity.
Both add behaviour to HTML without a virtual DOM.
differs: React moves the UI into the browser as code; htmx keeps it on the server as HTML.
Qwik renders on the server and resumes on the client; htmx stays on the server for every change.
htmx.pros: No build, no client state to keep in sync. Works with any backend language.
htmx.cons: Every interaction that changes state needs a server round trip. Rich client-only interactions (drag, offline, optimistic UI) need other tools.
